i Robots the satellites of the Ocean

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
cutting edge technology monitors climate change and fish stocks in the southern ocean

Summary:
South African scientists are making a major contribution to climate change research and monitoring fish stocks in the Southern Oceans through nine state of the art Ocean Gliders. These gliders, which look more like torpedoes, are diving to depths of 1000 meters at a time and when they surface for five minutes they transmit their data to climate change specialists and oceanographers’ computers on land. This cutting edge technology is revolutionising the amount of data we are able to collect in the Southern Oceans.

Further information:
CSIR's Marine Robotics programme is an exciting new development for South Africa and is a leader in its field competing with America, Norway and France on the cutting edge of scientific research.
The Southern Ocean has largely been studied for fish stocks but as the biggest body of water which stores 40% of all carbon emissions oceanographers and climate change experts and combining their research to understand more about the impacts of global warming, an South Africa is leading that research.

CSIR's Marine Robotics programme has developed two types of gliders: one that dives to 1000 meters called a buoyancy glider, and the other is a wave glider that stays on the surface measuring the interaction between the atmosphere and the ocean. Buoyancy gliders measure the amount of phytoplankton in the sea, the clarity and temperature and salinity of the ocean.

Plankton plays an important role in the oceanic carbon cycle by removing half of all CO2 from the atmosphere during photosynthesis – the process during which plants and other organisms convert light, usually from the Sun, into energy. The carbon then falls deep into the ocean and ends up on the sea bed, where it remains safely isolated from the atmosphere for centuries.

As well as being vital to climate control, it also creates enough oxygen for every other breath we take, and forms the base of the food chain for fisheries, so it is incredibly important for food security. Previous studies have shown that phytoplankton communities respond to global warming by changes in diversity and productivity. But the CSIR's Marine Robotics programme has shown that warmer temperatures directly impact the chemical cycles in plankton, which has not been shown before. It also underlines the important role of the Southern Ocean in global and regional climate regulation.

These gliders can be left at sea for six months at a time giving us the greatest amount of data. The wave gliders will be fitted with sonar so they can measure fish stocks and a camera so that scientist can identify the fish. Fish surveys traditionally happen once or twice a year and at great cost. Running the research ship, SA Agulhas 11, costs R300 000 a day, these gliders cost R3 million once off and can work all year around. The impact on fish surveys goes without saying - we will have a far more accurate picture and be able to set target catches for more precisely.

The other incredible thing about the gliders is that they act like satellites in the sea - they will be able to monitor fishing vessels and help us protect our fish stocks from poachers. Patagonian Toothfish, for example, are heavily poached in the Southern Ocean. At last maybe we have a riposte to Tina Joematt Petterson’s effective scuttling of our marine patrol vessels in Simon’s Town Harbour.

There is plenty of great footage from when they set the gliders to work close to the
Antarctic, underwater footage of the gliders at work. and fascinating graphics of phytoplankton concentrations, currents and atmospherics movement. We can also film them testing the gliders off False bay and see the fish stocks being monitored

Press Release:


Ocean gliders
Cutting edge robotic technology is revolutionising the way data is gathered from the Southern Ocean to monitor the effects of climate change. Carte Blanche meets South African scientists on a quest to unravel the mysteries locked in the world’s deepest oceans.


Script:


Script: This is one of the most extreme environments on earth. For the past three years an intrepid group of South Africa scientist has pushed the boundaries of data collected from the southern ocean. Launching ocean gliders off our polar icebreaker they are doing cutting edge climate change science
Seb: “it’s incredibly scary this little thing all on its own in these 10 meter seas.”
Script: Dr Sebastian Swart lead scientist of the Southern Ocean Climate and Carbon Observatory says they have even managed to get the gliders to tweet updates
Seb “Every time we get an update from the glider it feels like a bit of an Indiana Jones moment “
Link: Half of all human carbon emissions absorbed by the world’s oceans are taken up by the southern ocean, it’s extremely sensitive to climate change and yet it’s also an area of the planet we know the least about
Script: As part of the natural carbon cycle the Southern Ocean absorbs and releases CO2 into the atmosphere. However since the industrial era the ocean interior has stored 50 times more CO2 than the atmosphere so if things go out of balance it will have a dramatic impact on climate change. Dr Pedro Monteiro head of the Southern Oceans Climate and Carbon Observatory explains how the largest ocean on the planet functions

Pedro:” The southern ocean is driven by what is popularly known as the westerly winds so the westerly winds create this ring of water that circulates around the southern hemisphere
Essentially what you have is this cycle where deep CO2 is brought to the surface by the wind. So when it reaches the surface it outgases CO2 further north phytoplankton take up that CO2 and transport it into the ocean interior. “

Script: The plankton acts like a biological pump taking the CO2 down into the deep ocean but as the water is warming and getting more acidic due to global warming, combined with stronger winds and storms which are bringing more CO2 to the surface, the plankton can’t do its job as effectively

Pedro: “ So imagine this is a flywheel it is a slow turning but very big fly wheel, so the strengthening of those westerly winds imagine it begins to speed up this flywheel brings up more CO 2 but the additional warming associated with climate change reduces the primary productivity so the mechanism that brings it up is stronger but the mechanism that takes it down is weaker and that’s the problem”

Script: We have known this for the last 20 years but we haven’t had sufficient detailed information on the Southern Ocean to understand this process properly. Ocean robots are beginning to give us that detail

Pedro: “We understood from ship based measurements how the oceans varies on a big scale but what we didn’t understand was how fine scale dynamics let’s call it the weather in the ocean effect the sensitivity of the ocean to climate and the sensitivity of the climate to ocean”
Link: Our research vessel the SA Agulhas 2 is returning home after 3 months in the southern ocean and the Antarctic, on board is technology that can help unravel the mysteries around climate change and contribute to the fight to save the planet
Script: But ships are extremely expensive to operate. This polar breaker costs about R300 000 a day and only spends about 2 weeks of the year - in the summer months- gathering data. Ocean gliders on the other hand can be left at sea for up to six months at a fraction of the cost
Dr Seb Swart says the American designers told them they were crazy when they stated out 3 years ago

Seb: “But 2 to 3 years down the line we are really starting to see the success of those risky missions that we completed in the southern ocean. It’s a really scary place to work in and when we started our program we were really scared about what was the next thing that was going to be thrown at us. Some huge storms or ships that we have to avoid ice, ice is a big hazard in the southern ocean “

Script: In this little lab at the Waterfront they are pioneering a project that is creating a niche in climate change science

Seb:” We have 2 different kinds of gliders that profile the ocean they dive up and down from the surface to 1km depth and they have scientific instruments on them to measure the variables that we need to look at to understand what’s going on in the science. Then we have a second platform which we call a wave glider and that one stays on the surface and gets powered by the waves it moves around and collects data from the surface.”

Link: These ocean gliders are revolutionising climate science and oceanography another exciting element is that these two craft are being twinned to maximise the data collected from above and beneath the surface
Seb: “The atmosphere is interacting with the ocean all the time and before we didn’t really have an idea of how they were behaving together and now that we have measurements that extend all the way from the ocean to the atmosphere we can actually see the processes that are happening”

Script: The gliders are remotely controlled from Cape Town which now boasts some of the best glider pilots in the world who can navigate the most treacherous ocean conditions.

SEB “The gliders use satellite communications like GPS and meridian communications they basically call us so we are sitting in the office and the diving glider takes about 5 hours to do a dive and when it comes to the surface again it finds its connection with the satellite phones us gives us its data and we give it back signals and commands and actually change what the glider does”

Script: And it’s not only ice and strong currents they have to navigate. The coastal waters are filled with large container ships and fishing vessels that could easily mow them down

Seb: “The gliders are intelligent enough to tell us where the ships are. They have a sensor called an AIS which detects where the ships are and track where they are and move our glider accordingly”

Script: The ship can also only work in the summer months for about 2 weeks. But these gliders are working 6 months at a time and so they are getting a much more detailed picture
Seb “Here we have a shot of what is the temperature that the gliders measured between the surface ocean and to 1km so this is a complete picture of just that one glider observing the temperature of the ocean “
Link:The scientific Holy Grail is to gather information from the southern ocean in winter these wave gliders will be deployed from Cape Town for that very purpose and they will take about a month to get there
SEB: “So winter observations in the southern ocean until now have been either very difficult or impossible the conditions are just too rough getting data in the winter periods is really important to understanding the full seasonal scale elements of the science and research. Previously we just didn’t have a clue or any insight into what was going on there in winter”

Script: It’s clear these guys get really attached to their gliders, tracking them day in and out as they travel all alone in the massive ocean. Initially the gliders all had names like Pinkie , the Brain and Vader but that clouded the scientists objectivity so they are back to being numbers.
Seb “That is glider 542 that has been in the Antarctic for the last 3 months and you can see spatially where it has been sampling and it was continuously taking measurements and then about 2 weeks ago we needed it to go a little bit further south to intercept the ship so when the ship came it was in the right location for the ship to grab it out of the southern ocean and take it”
Script: And it’s a whole lot easier said than done. Intern Kagiso Mbete never imagined the weather could ever get that bad
Kagiso: “ The first time we tried to deploy the wave glider it actually hit back on the ship and we actually tried to abort the mission and then we tried again and it was fine but we had 8 meter swells and the boat was swinging and rolling so it was a mess “

Script: The latest spinoff off from the investment into developing the gliders is to use them for fish surveys in conjunction with fisheries research vessels. However the Fisheries vessels haven’t gone to sea for the last few years after former Fisheries Minister Tina Joematt Petersen handed them over to the navy
John. One of the great things about the gliders is that you can almost guarantee that they will be in the ocean unlike the ships
Janet “ Indeed we have had some problems with getting our research vessels back online after the fiasco we had with the decommissioning earlier”

Script: Fisheries scientist Janet Coetzee says the fish surveys are expensive costing about R50 million a survey and so they happen infrequently

Janet: “What we don’t know is what is happening between surveys and the advantage of using gliders is that they can be out there in the ocean continuously and they can be monitoring from your office”

Script: They can also be used to detect illegal fishing vessels in our waters
Script: So the idea is to release hundreds of gliders into the ocean, linking to hundreds of satellites which will inevitably generate mega data. The CSIR has acquired super computers to translate all this data into accessible information, one of which is the earth system model
Pedro: “One of the things we will be doing with our earth system model is not just understanding how changes in the southern ocean will effect global CO2 and climate but how that translates into regional climate how does it affect the winter rainfall in the Cape”
Script: This ocean glider project in the southern ocean is so unique that it has created a niche for SA in the global understanding of climate change. Up until recently the oceanic contribution to carbon emission wasn’t even factored into the models of climate change. Now, for the first time it will be part of the climate change talks
Pedro:” The real power is in bringing the gliders the super computer, the high resolution models in the super computer the ships and the satellites together…..and we are doing that as a South Africa interdisciplinary team to bring a unique contribution actually something that is different to what other institutions globally are doing. And that is going to be our contribution to the next global assessment of climate which is in 2019”
Script: If we don’t understand what impact the warming climate is having on the southern ocean and do something to stop it, when that CO2 fly wheel starts speeding up, it’s going to be impossible to stop.
Pedro: “The influence of the ocean in climate is still going to emerge in the 2nd half of the century, so we want to understand these dynamics now so that our decedents in the 2nd half of the century are actually in a position to make better decisions than we have”

Previously we just didn’t have a clue or any insight into what was going on there in winter” Script: It’s clear these guys get really attached to their gliders, tracking them day in and out as they travel all alone in the massive ocean. Initially the gliders all had names like Pinkie , the Brain and Vader but that clouded the scientists objectivity so they are back to being numbers. Seb “That is glider 542 that has been in the Antarctic for the last 3 months and you can see spatially where it has been sampling and it was continuously taking measurements and then about 2 weeks ago we needed it to go a little bit further south to intercept the ship so when the ship came it was in the right location for the ship to grab it out of the southern ocean and take it” Script: And it’s a whole lot easier said than done. Intern Kagiso Mbete never imagined the weather could ever get that bad Kagiso: “ The first time we tried to deploy the wave glider it actually hit back on the ship and we actually tried to abort the mission and then we tried again and it was fine but we had 8 meter swells and the boat was swinging and rolling so it was a mess “ Script: The latest spinoff off from the investment into developing the gliders is to use them for fish surveys in conjunction with fisheries research vessels. However the Fisheries vessels haven’t gone to sea for the last few years after former Fisheries Minister Tina Joematt Petersen handed them over to the navy John. One of the great things about the gliders is that you can almost guarantee that they will be in the ocean unlike the ships Janet “ Indeed we have had some problems with getting our research vessels back online after the fiasco we had with the decommissioning earlier” Script: Fisheries scientist Janet Coetzee says the fish surveys are expensive costing about R50 million a survey and so they happen infrequently Janet: “What we don’t know is what is happening between surveys and the advantage of using gliders is that they can be out there in the ocean continuously and they can be monitoring from your office” Script: They can also be used to detect illegal fishing vessels in our waters Script: So the idea is to release hundreds of gliders into the ocean, linking to hundreds of satellites which will inevitably generate mega data. The CSIR has acquired super computers to translate all this data into accessible information, one of which is the earth system model Pedro: “One of the things we will be doing with our earth system model is not just understanding how changes in the southern ocean will effect global CO2 and climate but how that translates into regional climate how does it affect the winter rainfall in the Cape” Script: This ocean glider project in the southern ocean is so unique that it has created a niche for SA in the global understanding of climate change. Up until recently the oceanic contribution to carbon emission wasn’t even factored into the models of climate change. Now, for the first time it will be part of the climate change talks Pedro:” The real power is in bringing the gliders the super computer, the high resolution models in the super computer the ships and the satellites together…..and we are doing that as a South Africa interdisciplinary team to bring a unique contribution actually something that is different to what other institutions globally are doing. And that is going to be our contribution to the next global assessment of climate which is in 2019” Script: If we don’t understand what impact the warming climate is having on the southern ocean and do something to stop it, when that CO2 fly wheel starts speeding up, it’s going to be impossible to stop. Pedro: “The influence of the ocean in climate is still going to emerge in the 2nd half of the century, so we want to understand these dynamics now so that our decedents in the 2nd half of the century are actually in a position to make better decisions than we have” Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for i Robots the satellites of the Ocean (4490 ) lizfish@iafrica.com 24 February 2015

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): cutting edge technology monitors climate change and fish stocks in the southern ocean
metadata.Summary: South African scientists are making a major contribution to climate change research and monitoring fish stocks in the Southern Oceans through nine state of the art Ocean Gliders. These gliders, which look more like torpedoes, are diving to depths of 1000 meters at a time and when they surface for five minutes they transmit their data to climate change specialists and oceanographers’ computers on land. This cutting edge technology is revolutionising the amount of data we are able to collect in the Southern Oceans.
metadata.Further information: CSIR's Marine Robotics programme is an exciting new development for South Africa and is a leader in its field competing with America, Norway and France on the cutting edge of scientific research. The Southern Ocean has largely been studied for fish stocks but as the biggest body of water which stores 40% of all carbon emissions oceanographers and climate change experts and combining their research to understand more about the impacts of global warming, an South Africa is leading that research. CSIR's Marine Robotics programme has developed two types of gliders: one that dives to 1000 meters called a buoyancy glider, and the other is a wave glider that stays on the surface measuring the interaction between the atmosphere and the ocean. Buoyancy gliders measure the amount of phytoplankton in the sea, the clarity and temperature and salinity of the ocean. Plankton plays an important role in the oceanic carbon cycle by removing half of all CO2 from the atmosphere during photosynthesis – the process during which plants and other organisms convert light, usually from the Sun, into energy. The carbon then falls deep into the ocean and ends up on the sea bed, where it remains safely isolated from the atmosphere for centuries. As well as being vital to climate control, it also creates enough oxygen for every other breath we take, and forms the base of the food chain for fisheries, so it is incredibly important for food security. Previous studies have shown that phytoplankton communities respond to global warming by changes in diversity and productivity. But the CSIR's Marine Robotics programme has shown that warmer temperatures directly impact the chemical cycles in plankton, which has not been shown before. It also underlines the important role of the Southern Ocean in global and regional climate regulation. These gliders can be left at sea for six months at a time giving us the greatest amount of data. The wave gliders will be fitted with sonar so they can measure fish stocks and a camera so that scientist can identify the fish. Fish surveys traditionally happen once or twice a year and at great cost. Running the research ship, SA Agulhas 11, costs R300 000 a day, these gliders cost R3 million once off and can work all year around. The impact on fish surveys goes without saying - we will have a far more accurate picture and be able to set target catches for more precisely. The other incredible thing about the gliders is that they act like satellites in the sea - they will be able to monitor fishing vessels and help us protect our fish stocks from poachers. Patagonian Toothfish, for example, are heavily poached in the Southern Ocean. At last maybe we have a riposte to Tina Joematt Petterson’s effective scuttling of our marine patrol vessels in Simon’s Town Harbour. There is plenty of great footage from when they set the gliders to work close to the Antarctic, underwater footage of the gliders at work. and fascinating graphics of phytoplankton concentrations, currents and atmospherics movement. We can also film them testing the gliders off False bay and see the fish stocks being monitored
